items.title: The Negotiation
items.reason: A failed opening hostage rescue leaves police negotiator Ha Chae-youn shaken before an arms dealer, Min Tae-gu, demands to speak exclusively with her during a new hostage crisis. Across the complete film, his apparently arbitrary demands expose a progressively more complicated scheme: one apparent journalist is an undercover intelligence agent, a supposedly straightforward kidnapping is linked to an earlier killing, the hostage taker's personal motive emerges, and compromised police, political and corporate officials try to suppress evidence and manage a raid. Each discovery changes the negotiator's understanding of whom she can trust and what Min is trying to accomplish. The central engine is psychological bargaining over a video link rather than a conventional culprit hunt or sustained physical action; the later action and military response are episodic. Yonhap describes gradually revealed intentions and successive twists, while Cinema Escapist highlights recurring information and brisk tension. The contrary critical evidence matters: Rotten Tomatoes quotes reviews faulting a predictable corruption story, implausible institutional behavior, stretches of talk and an exposition-heavy final act. Thus the movie's cat-and-mouse and suspense are stronger than its clue-puzzling or perfectly even revelation cadence. Its arms-dealer background and security response do not make it a military-operations-first film.

items.title: The Dry
items.reason: Federal investigator Aaron Falk returns to his drought-stricken hometown after a friend's apparent family murder-suicide and reopens an older mystery about the drowning of a teenage girl. The 117-minute film develops two intertwined investigations through scene reconstruction, ammunition that does not match the family's weapons, CCTV, hostile witnesses, memories of an old alibi, a note marked 'grant?' and school-funding documents. The meaning of 'grant' changes from a suspect's name to financial funding, redirecting suspicion toward embezzlement; a late confession resolves the recent murders, and the girl's recovered diary reframes the decades-old death. The full IMDb synopsis supports these clues across the opening, middle and end, while RogerEbert.com specifically notes that fragmented flashbacks slowly supply information and encourage the viewer to interpret evidence. The Guardian praises polished, gripping suspense but notes a succession of red herrings and reveals near the end. Investigation and clue-puzzling are therefore high, yet revelation frequency is more moderate than the dual-mystery premise alone might suggest: atmosphere, grief, community hostility and flashback drama occupy significant runtime, and the biggest answers are backloaded. The film is a slow-burning small-town mystery rather than an action-heavy chase or psychological duel. The cinematography and dusty landscape are deliberate high-quality craft, not a cheap presentation.
